analysis.one_liner: Quadruples the excise tax on corporate stock buybacks and closes an executive-pay loophole.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the stock buyback tax from 1% to 4% has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote since its June 2026 introduction, with all seven of its supporters being Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: Corporations already pay a 1% federal tax when they buy back their own stock, and they can lower that tax by the value of new stock they issue — including stock handed to executives. This bill would quadruple the tax to 4% and stop stock issued to executives or anyone earning over $1 million a year from counting against it. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has seen no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal government would collect more revenue from corporations that buy back their own stock, since the excise tax rate would rise from 1% to 4% [S2]. Shareholders other than top executives benefit from closing the offset loophole: under current law, a company can issue stock to its highest-paid people and use that issuance to reduce or erase its buyback tax; the bill stops stock issued to covered executives or anyone paid over $1 million from counting toward that reduction [S2]. To the extent a higher tax slows buybacks, companies may direct more cash to hiring, investment, or wages — though the record here contains no estimate of those effects.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1% to 4%, applying to repurchases after enactment [S2].
It closes an offset: stock issued to covered executives or to anyone earning more than $1 million in a year can no longer be used to reduce a company's buyback tax liability [S2].

The higher rate and the executive exception together mean companies buying back large amounts of stock while simultaneously issuing shares to top earners would pay substantially more tax than under current law [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that repurchase their own stock pay the higher 4% tax, and the largest new costs fall on companies that both buy back shares and issue stock to highly paid executives, who lose the offset [S2]. If companies respond by cutting back buybacks, shareholders — including mutual funds, pensions, and 401(k) investors — could see modestly lower returns from that channel, and some companies may shift cash to dividends, which are taxed as income to recipients.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies buying back their own stock

drawbacks.text: A 4% tax on repurchases raises the cost of a common way for companies to return excess cash to shareholders; some of that cost can land on retirement savers and pension funds that own the stock, through reduced buyback-driven returns [S2].

Because companies can shift cash to dividends or debt-financed payouts, a buyback tax changes the form of payouts more than it raises revenue, and the executive-pay exception adds administrative complexity without touching stock issued to lower-paid employees, which still offsets the tax [S2].
The record here contains no revenue estimate or economic analysis of the higher rate, so the actual gain to the public cannot be sized from these sources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, targeted change: it makes a specific corporate tax avoidance channel more expensive rather than banning buybacks. The benefit — more revenue and less tax-free executive stock recycling — is real but unquantified in the record; the cost is some distortion in how companies return cash, with part of the burden possibly landing on ordinary shareholders through retirement funds. The biggest design gap is the lack of any revenue or incidence analysis in the sources.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee has taken no action since.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the Stock Buyback Accountability Act of 2026 in the Senate on June 16, 2026, joined by Sens. Wyden, Warren, Reed, Van Hollen, Markey, and Whitehouse [S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S1].
The complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S4].
All seven sponsors and cosponsors on record are Democrats, with no Republican support listed [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, corporations that buy back stock keep the current 1% rate, and companies issuing stock to highly paid executives keep the ability to use those issuances to reduce their buyback tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Stock-buying corporations and highly paid executives

for.name: Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 16, 2026, and recruited six Democratic Senate cosponsors.

for.name: Ron Wyden and six other Democratic senators (Warren, Reed, Van Hollen, Markey, Whitehouse, and one additional cosponsor)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a unified Democratic Senate backing but no Republican support.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 16, 2026, and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats [S3]; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee has not acted on the bill [S4].

industries.industry: Public companies that repurchase their own stock
industries.note: The bill would quadruple their excise tax from 1% to 4% on net share repurchases [S2]. Their interest in avoiding the tax runs against the public interest in revenue and in discouraging buybacks timed around executive compensation.

industries.industry: Highly paid corporate executives receiving stock compensation
industries.note: Under current law, a company's issuance of stock to executives can offset its buyback tax; the bill removes that offset for covered executives and anyone paid over $1 million, making this group's compensation costlier for their employers to fund alongside buybacks [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in the Senate Finance Committee for months with no hearing and no Republican cosponsors rarely advance before a Congress ends. With Republicans holding the Senate majority and the session closing on January 3, 2027, the most likely outcome is that the bill dies in committee without a vote, and its sponsor would need to reintroduce it in the next Congress.
